2:
SAY:
- Read the cultural sensitivity statement aloud, in a calm voice.
- 'Today we are learning about the Coorong, which sits on Ngarrindjeri Country.'
- 'We acknowledge their custodianship of this land.'

DO:
- Pause briefly so students take it in.
- Move on without inviting discussion.

TEACHER NOTES:
Deliver as a one-minute orientation. Not a discussion task.

SENSITIVITY ADVISORY:
- What it is: references to deceased persons, historical perspectives, and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander histories and cultures, including Ngarrindjeri Country.
- Framing language: see SAY.
- Watch for: students who may have personal or cultural connections; signs of discomfort.
- Protocol: pause if a student is distressed, offer a quiet seat or water, let the student step out and rejoin without comment.

WATCH FOR:
- Body language at the moment of reading.

[Stage: Lesson Orientation]
7:
SAY:
- 'Today we are planning a body paragraph for an information report about the Coorong.'
- Read each Success Criterion aloud and point as you go.
- 'If planning paragraphs feels new, that is okay. We will build it together.'

DO:
- Point to each SC.
- Tap the planning criterion twice so students hold it as today's writing focus.

TEACHER NOTES:
This lesson plans body paragraph 3 (Flora and Fauna). Lesson 20 turns the plan into a written paragraph.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who cannot say the planning goal back; flag for extra modelling at slides 32 to 36.

[Stage: LI and SC]
8:
SAY:
- 'On your desk: pencil, booklet and novel, mini whiteboard and texta.'
- 'Thumbs up when you are ready.'

DO:
- Scan for thumbs.

TEACHER NOTES:
Ready-to-learn check.

[Stage: Materials]
9:
SAY:
- 'We are about to read a non-fiction text about the Coorong. This is the background knowledge we need for our information report.'

DO:
- Display and move on.

TEACHER NOTES:
Section divider. Non-fiction reading is the source for SDs.

[Stage: Background Knowledge]
10:
SOURCES:
- Coorong National Park Teacher Resource Pack, pages 16 to 19.

SAY:
- 'This is our non-fiction text. It tells us about the flora and fauna of the Coorong.'
- 'Listen for the kinds of plants and animals that live there - we will need these later.'

DO:
- Frame the reading.
- The next slides summarise the text.

TEACHER NOTES:
Focus pages: 16 to 19.

[Stage: I Do | Text Launch]
11:
SAY:
- 'Read the text with me. Flora of Coorong National Park.'
- 'Listen for: how many plant species, where some came from, and what has happened to wetland habitat.'

DO:
- Choral or read-aloud, your choice.
- Mark or annotate keywords on screen if your set-up allows: 353 species, 132 non-native, 5 rare.
- Ask: 'What did you notice about wetland habitat?'

TEACHER NOTES:
The figures are useful for SDs.

[Stage: We Do | Read]
12:
SAY:
- 'Read with me. The Bonney Upwelling.'
- 'A marine event between Portland and Robe. Cold water from Antarctica moves up onto the continental shelf and brings nutrients.'
- Ask: 'Why does that matter?' Expected: 'Sunlight turns nutrients into food for marine animals.'

DO:
- Choral or read-aloud.
- Pause to anchor the term Bonney Upwelling.

TEACHER NOTES:
The Bonney Upwelling is one of the SDs in the modelled SPO.

WATCH FOR:
- Students lost in technical detail; rephrase: 'Cold water comes up from the deep, brings food, animals thrive.'

[Stage: We Do | Read]
13:
SAY:
- 'Three groups of plants in the Coorong. Read with me.'
- 'Terrestrial - dry land, cannot survive being underwater.'
- 'Amphibious - adapted to both wet and dry.'
- 'Submerged - need to be underwater to survive.'

DO:
- Read aloud or choral.
- Have students mime: dry-land hands, alternating wet-dry hands, fully under hands.

TEACHER NOTES:
Three useful categories for students writing about plants.

[Stage: We Do | Read]
14:
SAY:
- 'Read with me. The vegetation on the Younghusband Peninsula.'
- 'Listen for: native plants and non-native invasive plants.'

DO:
- Choral or read-aloud.
- Pause on '30% non-native' - that is a usable statistic.

WATCH FOR:
- Long lists of plant names; not every name needs to stick. Highlight the categories.

[Stage: We Do | Read]
15:
SAY:
- 'Read with me. Ruppia tuberosa.'
- 'A crucial aquatic plant in the Coorong. Provides food for waterbirds and habitat for fish.'
- 'A drought caused a rapid decline. The Ruppia Translocation Project moves seeds back to help recovery.'

DO:
- Choral or read-aloud.
- Highlight the cause-and-effect: drought leads-to decline; action leads-to recovery.

[Stage: We Do | Read]
16:
SAY:
- 'Read with me. Birds of the Coorong.'
- 'Listen for: the number of species, year-round residents, and migratory shorebirds that travel from Alaska and Siberia.'

DO:
- Choral or read-aloud.
- Highlight: 85 species, migratory birds from Alaska and Siberia.

WATCH FOR:
- Students intimidated by bird names; we want categories, not memorisation.

[Stage: We Do | Read]
17:
SAY:
- 'Read with me. Pelican breeding and human impact.'
- 'Pelicans nest on islands. 3000 to 4000 in a good season.'
- 'Australia has lost half its wetlands in 200 years. Fishing lines, pollution and 4WDs harm the birds.'

DO:
- Choral or read-aloud.
- Pause to anchor 'half its wetlands' - this is a concerning fact students can use.

WATCH FOR:
- Reactions to pelican facts (they are central to Storm Boy); use to build connection.

[Stage: We Do | Read]
18:
SAY:
- 'Read with me. Mammals of the Coorong.'
- 'Native: seals, sea lions, echidnas, wombats, possums, bats, kangaroos, wallabies, native rats. Some are rare or vulnerable.'
- 'Non-native: cats, foxes, hares, deer, rabbits.'
- 'Long-nosed fur seals are recent visitors and have impacted local fishers and the Ngarrindjeri people.'

DO:
- Choral or read-aloud.
- Pause on the Ngarrindjeri reference - acknowledge the traditional owners briefly.

[Stage: We Do | Read]
19:
SAY:
- 'Read with me. Reptiles and amphibians.'
- 'Reptiles: lizards and snakes. The heath goanna is vulnerable.'
- 'Amphibians: frogs help control algae and provide food for birds.'

DO:
- Choral or read-aloud.
- Highlight the role of frogs in the ecosystem.

[Stage: We Do | Read]
20:
SAY:
- 'Read with me. Fish and other invertebrates.'
- '93 fish species. Non-native carp, perch, mosquito fish have affected native populations.'
- 'In conclusion: Coorong National Park hosts a rich and diverse array of fauna. Conservation is essential.'

DO:
- Choral or read-aloud.
- Wrap with: 'We will use these facts in our SPO.'

[Stage: We Do | Read]
21:
SAY:
- 'Why is the Ruppia tuberosa a crucial aquatic plant in the Coorong?'
- 'Show me on your fingers. Select all that apply.'
- 'One: it is an endangered species. Two: it provides food for water birds. Three: it provides habitat and nourishment for fish. Four: it improves the water quality.'
- Ask: 'Three, two, one, show.' Expected: 2 and 3.

DO:
- Scan boards.
- Ask: 'Why two and three?' Look for direct quotes from the text.

CFU CHECKPOINT:
Technique: Show Fingers 1-4
Script:
- 'Show me which options apply.'
- Scan for: clear majority on 2 and 3.
PROCEED:
- Confirm 2 and 3 with a re-read of the Ruppia slide.
PIVOT:
- Most likely misconception: students pick 1 (endangered) because they have heard the word.
- Reteach with the rule: 'The text says crucial, not endangered. Read for what is said.'
- Re-check: 'Show me again.'

WATCH FOR:
- Students who pick all four; redirect to evidence in the text.

[Stage: CFU | Comprehension]
22:
SAY:
- 'What is integral to maintain the balance of the ecosystem? Show me on your fingers.'
- 'One: conservation efforts. Two: increased employment. Three: rain. Four: minimal pollution.'
- Ask: 'Three, two, one, show.' Expected: 1.

DO:
- Scan boards.
- Ask: 'Why one?' Expected: 'the text says conservation efforts are essential.'

CFU CHECKPOINT:
Technique: Show Fingers 1-4
Script:
- 'Which is integral to balance? Show me.'
- Scan for: clear majority on 1.
PROCEED:
- Confirm 1 and tie back to the closing sentence of the non-fiction text.
PIVOT:
- Most likely misconception: students pick 4 (minimal pollution) because it is an environmental answer.
- Reteach with the rule: 'Pollution matters, but the text says conservation efforts are essential. Use the text wording.'
- Re-check: 'Show me again.'

WATCH FOR:
- Students choosing 3 (rain).

[Stage: CFU | Comprehension]
23:
SAY:
- 'Now we move to writing. We are planning a body paragraph for our information report on the Coorong.'

DO:
- Display and move on.

TEACHER NOTES:
Section divider. The SPO frame from lesson 17 is the same plan tool used here.

[Stage: Text-Level Writing]
24:
SAY:
- 'Watch this first.'
- 'An information report aims to inform the reader by classifying or describing factual information about a specific topic.'
- 'The purpose is to teach the reader, not to persuade them or tell a story.'
- 'I am going to model planning a body paragraph soon.'

DO:
- Read the purpose aloud.
- Contrast briefly: 'Storm Boy is a story. An information report is facts.'

TEACHER NOTES:
Anchor the genre.

[Stage: I Do | Genre Purpose]
25:
SAY:
- 'Our topic is the Coorong. Today we are planning the body paragraph about flora and fauna.'
- 'Flora means plants. Fauna means animals.'
- 'Watch this first - we will use the SPO frame to plan.'

DO:
- Frame the focus.
- Click any link to mentor text if your class needs a model paragraph.

TEACHER NOTES:
Today's paragraph is body paragraph 3.

[Stage: I Do | Topic Frame]
26:
SAY:
- 'An information report has these parts. Read with me.'
- 'Title. Introduction. Body paragraph one, two and three. Conclusion.'
- 'We will be planning body paragraph three using a Single Paragraph Outline.'
- Ask: 'Where does our paragraph fit?' Expected: 'body paragraph three.'

DO:
- Point to each part as you read it.
- Cold call one student.

TEACHER NOTES:
Framing the report structure. Students need to see the whole before they plan a part.

WATCH FOR:
- Students confusing factual recount with information report; clarify only if it surfaces.

[Stage: We Do | Structure]
27:
SAY:
- 'Watch this first. I will mark the topic sentence, supporting details and concluding sentence in this paragraph.'
- 'TS: The Coorong ecosystem is unique and complex, home to many vulnerable and endangered species.'
- 'SDs are about wetland removal, migratory birds from Alaska and Siberia, and the Bonney Upwelling.'
- 'CS: The Coorong is a rich environment teeming with various local and migratory species unlike anywhere else in the world.'
- 'Notice: the CS echoes the TS without copying it.'

DO:
- Highlight TS, SDs and CS as you go.
- Use the colour coding chart referenced in your existing notes.

TEACHER NOTES:
Show how the parts work together in a real paragraph.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who think every sentence is supporting; only the middle sentences are SDs.

[Stage: I Do | Paragraph Parts]
28:
SAY:
- 'Which option should be in a concluding sentence? Show me on your fingers.'
- 'One: details about events. Two: extra information. Three: the writer's opinion. Four: summary of the main ideas.'
- Ask: 'Three, two, one, show.' Expected: 4.

DO:
- Scan boards.
- Ask: 'Why four?' Expected: 'because a CS summarises and closes the paragraph.'

CFU CHECKPOINT:
Technique: Show Fingers 1-4
Script:
- 'Show me what a CS does.'
- Scan for: clear majority on 4.
PROCEED:
- Confirm 4.
PIVOT:
- Most likely misconception: students pick 3 (opinion) because they have written persuasive paragraphs before.
- Reteach with the rule: 'Information reports give facts, not opinions.'
- Re-check: 'Show me again.'

WATCH FOR:
- Students who pick 1 (details); details are SDs, not the CS.

[Stage: CFU | CS]
29:
SAY:
- 'A topic sentence does four things. Watch this first.'
- 'Introduces the main idea of the paragraph.'
- 'Helps to keep your writing clear and organised.'
- 'Grabs the reader's attention.'
- 'Tells the reader what to expect.'

DO:
- Click to reveal each.
- Read your TS example again so students hear what the four jobs sound like.

TEACHER NOTES:
Review before students write their own.

[Stage: I Do | TS Purpose]
30:
SAY:
- 'TS: The Coorong ecosystem is unique and complex, home to many vulnerable and endangered species.'
- 'This TS tells us who the Coorong is home to and uses adjectives - unique, complex, vulnerable, endangered - to build description.'
- Ask: 'On your whiteboards, draw a circle around any adjective in the TS. Three, two, one, show.'

DO:
- Scan boards. Look for unique, complex, vulnerable, endangered.
- Ask: 'Which adjective gives the strongest picture?'

WATCH FOR:
- Students who do not know what an adjective is; quick reminder - describing words.

[Stage: We Do | TS]
31:
SAY:
- 'Three TS examples. Read each with me.'
- Read all three options chorally.
- Ask: 'Whiteboards: write the option you would use, and one reason. Three minutes.'

DO:
- Circulate; read several boards.
- Cold call non-volunteers to share.
- Emphasise that all three are valid; the TS just needs to introduce the main idea.

TEACHER NOTES:
These options can be given to students who need a TS scaffold for their booklet task.

WATCH FOR:
- Students copying option one without thinking; push for the reason.

[Stage: We Do | TS]
32:
SAY:
- 'Supporting details do four things. Watch this first.'
- 'Give examples. Help to keep your writing clear and organised. Include reasons. Provide facts.'
- 'I am about to model finding SDs from the non-fiction text.'

DO:
- Click to reveal each.
- Frame the next slide as the I Do for finding SDs.

[Stage: I Do | SD Purpose]
33:
SAY:
- 'Watch this first. The TS is given. I am going to find a supporting detail from the non-fiction text.'
- 'I read: the large-scale removal of wetlands has reduced habitat for many species.'
- 'Keywords: removal of wetlands, reduced plants and wildlife, reliant on area.'
- 'My note: removal of local wetland equals down arrow plants and wildlife leads-to reliant upon area.'
- 'Notice the symbols and short phrases - this is the SPO note form we use.'

DO:
- Click to reveal the note.
- Tap the SPO chart from lesson 18.

TEACHER NOTES:
Note the use of last lesson's shorthand techniques.

WATCH FOR:
- Students copying full sentences; redirect to note form.

[Stage: I Do | Find SD1]
34:
SAY:
- 'We do one together. Read this passage about waterbirds with me.'
- 'Over 85 species of waterbirds. Migratory shorebirds like the red-necked stint, sharp-tailed sandpiper, curlew sandpiper. From Alaska and Siberia.'
- Ask: 'On your whiteboards, write SD2 in note form. Use shorthand. Three minutes.'

DO:
- Circulate; read several boards.
- Reveal: 'home leads-to birds & migratory species leads-to Alaska & Siberia.'
- Cold call one student.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who write the full sentence.

[Stage: We Do | Find SD2]
35:
SAY:
- 'You do one. Read about the Bonney Upwelling.'
- 'When spring winds shift to the southeast, an ocean current causes surface water to drift offshore. Cold, nutrient-rich water from Antarctica wells up. Sunlight turns those nutrients into food for marine species.'
- Ask: 'On your whiteboards, write SD3 in note form using shorthand. Three minutes.'

DO:
- Circulate; read several boards.
- Reveal: 'Bonney Upwelling leads-to up arrow water leads-to Antarctica leads-to leaves nutrients leads-to marine animals = require for survival.'
- Cold call one student.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who write 'Bonney Upwelling is a marine event' as a full sentence.

[Stage: You Do | Find SD3]
36:
SAY:
- 'Now we have all three SDs. Read the SPO with me.'
- Choral read each line of the SPO.
- 'Notice the brevity. Each SD provides one fact.'

DO:
- Choral read the SPO.
- Acknowledge the structure: TS plus three SDs.

TEACHER NOTES:
This is the modelled plan students will replicate in the booklet. You may also delete the text and model live with your own SDs if your class is ready.

[Stage: We Do | SPO Build]
37:
SAY:
- 'Three options. Which SD matches this TS?'
- 'TS: The Coorong is renowned for its diverse and abundant birdlife, providing critical habitat for both resident and migratory species.'
- 'Item one: vital breeding ground for numerous bird species, including the iconic Australian pelican.'
- 'Item two: extensive plant communities, including salt marshes and shrub lands.'
- 'Item three: popular tourist destination, attracting visitors with scenic landscapes.'
- Ask: 'Show me one, two or three. Three, two, one, show.' Expected: 1.

DO:
- Scan boards.
- Ask: 'Why item one?' Expected: 'matches the topic of birdlife and habitat.'

CFU CHECKPOINT:
Technique: Show Fingers 1-3
Script:
- 'Show me which SD matches the TS.'
- Scan for: clear majority on 1.
PROCEED:
- Confirm 1.
PIVOT:
- Most likely misconception: students pick 3 (tourist destination) because the Coorong has tourism.
- Reteach with the rule: 'Read the TS first. The TS is about birdlife. SDs must support birdlife specifically.'
- Re-check: 'Show me again.'

WATCH FOR:
- Students who think any fact about the Coorong is a supporting detail.

[Stage: CFU | SD Match]
38:
SAY:
- 'On your whiteboards, record three supporting details for our paragraph on the Coorong.'
- 'Use your notes from earlier. Use the question prompts.'
- 'How many plant species, and where did they come from? What are the categories of plants? What animals migrate, and from where? How are plants and animals reliant on the area? What aids their survival?'
- 'Five minutes.'

DO:
- Time the work.
- Circulate; read first 3 students' boards.
- Pull a small group if students cannot generate any SDs.
- Print copies of the supplementary text from earlier slides for students who need them.

ENABLING & EXTENDING:
ENABLING PROMPT:
- Task: provide three pre-written SD options; students choose and add their own shorthand.
- Extra Notes: pair with a partner.
EXTENDING PROMPT:
- Task: write four SDs and choose the best three. Justify the cut.

TEACHER NOTES:
Use student work to plan the booklet support.

WATCH FOR:
- Students copying SDs from the modelled SPO.

[Stage: You Do | SDs]
39:
SAY:
- 'Watch this first. A concluding sentence summarises the main ideas of the paragraph and links with the topic sentence.'
- 'CS: The Coorong is a rich environment teeming with various local and migratory species unlike anywhere else in the world.'
- 'Notice: it summarises without repeating the TS word for word.'
- 'I need to check that my CS pulls together the SDs.'

DO:
- Read the CS aloud.
- Compare to the TS - point out what is echoed (unique, species) and what is added (rich, teeming).

TEACHER NOTES:
Next slide is the We Do.

[Stage: I Do | CS]
40:
SAY:
- 'Brainstorm key words for your concluding sentence.'
- 'Words on the slide: habitat restoration, biodiversity, species survival, protection, impact on environment, unique, important.'
- Ask: 'Whiteboards: write three or four key words you would use. Two minutes.'
- 'Then share with your partner one CS idea using those words.'

DO:
- Time the work.
- Cold call two pairs to share their CS ideas.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who write a full CS without picking key words first.

[Stage: We Do | CS]
41:
SAY:
- 'Read the SPO. Is this CS appropriate?'
- 'TS is about the Coorong ecosystem being unique and home to vulnerable and endangered species.'
- 'CS: Tourism development in the Coorong should be expanded to boost the local economy.'
- Ask: 'Thumbs up if it works, thumbs down if not. Three, two, one, show.' Expected: thumbs down.

DO:
- Scan thumbs.
- Ask: 'Why does it not work?' Expected: 'because it talks about tourism and money, not plants and animals.'

CFU CHECKPOINT:
Technique: Thumbs Up or Down
Script:
- 'Does this CS work? Thumbs up or down.'
- Scan for: clear majority on thumbs down.
PROCEED:
- Move to the booklet task.
PIVOT:
- Most likely misconception: students think any sentence about the Coorong fits.
- Reteach with the rule: 'A CS must echo the TS and pull the SDs together.'
- Re-check: 'Show me again.'

WATCH FOR:
- Students who say thumbs up because the sentence sounds nice.

[Stage: CFU | CS]
42:
SAY:
- 'Open your booklet to Lesson 19 - Plan a body paragraph for an information report.'
- 'Plan your body paragraph using the SPO frame: TS, three SDs in note form, CS.'
- 'Use the modelled examples as a scaffold or write your own.'
- 'Until the closing.'

DO:
- Set timer.
- Circulate; check the TS first for each student.
- Pull a small group for re-modelling on TS or SDs.

ENABLING & EXTENDING:
ENABLING PROMPT:
- Task: provide a TS and CS; students fill in just the three SDs.
- Extra Notes: provide the trimmed non-fiction text on paper.
EXTENDING PROMPT:
- Task: plan two SPOs - one on flora, one on fauna. Compare which SPO is stronger.

TEACHER NOTES:
The booklet task is the You Do for the planning objective. Lesson 20 turns this plan into a written paragraph.

WATCH FOR:
- TS that is too vague.
- SDs written as full sentences instead of notes.
- CS that copies the TS.

[Stage: You Do | Booklet]
44:
SAY:
- 'Read the model introduction with me.'
- Choral read the introduction.
- 'Notice: the introduction names the topic, says where it is, and sets up the body paragraphs.'
- 'Look for the GST formula - General, Specific, Technical.'

DO:
- Choral read.
- Highlight the GST structure if you have used the formula in earlier lessons.

TEACHER NOTES:
Use to show students what their full report will look like by lesson 20.

[Stage: Mentor Text | Introduction]
45:
SAY:
- 'Read body paragraph one with me. The topic is what the Coorong is and where it is located.'
- 'Notice: the paragraph follows the SPO structure - TS, SDs, CS.'
- 'Look for the GST formula in this paragraph.'

DO:
- Choral read the paragraph.
- Highlight the TS, SDs and CS as you go.

[Stage: Mentor Text | Body 1]
46:
SAY:
- 'Read body paragraph two with me. The topic is the cultural significance of the Coorong.'
- 'Notice the use of the Ngarrindjeri name Kurangk and the 2009 KNY agreement - those are precise facts.'

DO:
- Choral read the paragraph.
- Pause to acknowledge the Ngarrindjeri custodianship.

TEACHER NOTES:
Link back to the cultural sensitivity slide at the start.

[Stage: Mentor Text | Body 2]
47:
SAY:
- 'Read body paragraph three with me. This is the paragraph we just planned.'
- 'Notice how the SDs we built turn into full sentences in this model paragraph.'
- 'Lesson 20 will show us how to expand our SDs into sentences.'

DO:
- Choral read the paragraph.
- Highlight the TS, SDs and CS.

TEACHER NOTES:
This is the model students will work toward in lesson 20.

[Stage: Mentor Text | Body 3]
48:
SAY:
- 'Read the conclusion with me.'
- 'This report detailed the location of the Coorong and its cultural and ecological significance.'
- 'Notice: the conclusion summarises the whole report, not just one paragraph.'

DO:
- Choral read.
- Tap the GST formula one more time.

TEACHER NOTES:
Full report mentor text.

[Stage: Mentor Text | Conclusion]
